design_detail: Prospective cohort analysis of the PATH Study (US national probability cohort), Waves 1 to 4 (September 2013 to January 2018), public-use files. Adults aged 18 or older with no respiratory condition at baseline were classed by baseline self-reported e-cigarette status (never; former, which includes any past use even 1 or 2 puffs; current, every day or some days) and followed for newly self-reported diagnoses of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), emphysema, chronic bronchitis and asthma, singly and as a composite. Poisson regression gave incidence rate ratios, with sequential adjustment and sensitivity analyses.
can_establish: How the rate of newly self-reported respiratory diagnoses over up to about four years compared, after adjustment for demographics, smoking history, other tobacco, other drugs, body mass index and chronic conditions, between US adults who had ever used e-cigarettes at baseline (former or current) and adults who had never used them.
cannot_establish: Whether e-cigarettes cause any respiratory condition (observational; baseline-only exposure; smoking history adjusted by broad categories, so residual confounding is likely), whether the same holds for devices since 2014, how much risk comes from current versus past use, or measured lung function (all outcomes are self-reported diagnoses).

sample.recruitment: PATH Study, a national longitudinal survey begun in 2013 by NIH and FDA, oversampling people who use tobacco, young adults (18 to 24) and African American adults. Wave 1 data were collected from 12 September 2013 to 14 December 2014 and Wave 4 from 1 December 2016 to 3 January 2018. Retention of the Wave 1 cohort was 83.2% at Wave 2, 78.4% at Wave 3 and 73.5% at Wave 4 (Methods › Study Setting). Excluded: a baseline respiratory condition, loss to follow-up by Wave 2, missing e-cigarette data; sample sizes differ by condition (Table 2). The selection flow chart (eFigure 1) was not read.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Adults 18 or older at baseline without COPD, emphysema, chronic bronchitis or asthma; at least one follow-up wave; e-cigarette status known. Youth who aged into the adult sample and Wave 4 replenishment respondents were not included.
sample.demographics: 49.1% men, 65.2% non-Hispanic White, 11.5% Black, 15.5% Hispanic, 7.9% other; weighted age spread even from 18-24 (13.1%) to 65 and over (16.9%); mean baseline pack-years 6.7 (Results › Baseline Characteristics, 1st paragraph; Table 1). People who currently used e-cigarettes were younger (21.9% aged 18-24 against 10.8% of people who had never used them) and much more likely to have smoked cigarettes: 16.0% had never smoked cigarettes against 72.1% of those who had never used e-cigarettes (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Retention fell to 73.5% by Wave 4; people lost after Wave 2 are censored at the wave of loss, and the extent of loss by e-cigarette group is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Baseline-only classification and exclusion of anyone with an existing respiratory condition. At baseline 7,405 (16.8% weighted) had ever used e-cigarettes; 'former' use includes people who had tried them for 1 or 2 puffs. Among people who currently used e-cigarettes, only 401 had never smoked cigarettes, so any analysis in never smokers rests on small numbers (the authors report one in the supplement, which was not read).

exposure.measurement: Self-report at Wave 1 only. Current = uses every day or some days; former = ever used, even 1 or 2 puffs, and not now; never = never used. Exploratory sub-division by every day vs some days, age at first use (under 25, 25 to 44, 45 or over) and experimental vs established use (used 'fairly regularly' or not).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Exposure is baseline status only; the authors state that time-varying exposure was not considered (Limitations). Device generation and flavors were not available for the first wave. In the exploratory analyses the highest incidence was in groups with every-day current use, first use before age 25, and established use (eFigure 2, values not read).
exposure.polysubstance: Cigarette smoking history adjusted as: never; former (quit under 5, 5 to 20, 20 or more years ago); current (under 5, 5 to 20, 20 or more pack-years). Ever use of cigars, cigarillos, pipe, hookah; ever use of heroin, inhalants or hallucinogens. Marijuana, second-hand smoke, childhood smoke exposure and smokeless tobacco were added only in sensitivity analyses (results in a supplement, not read).

comparison.controls: Adults who had never used an e-cigarette (not even 1 or 2 puffs), n = 14,213.
comparison.matching: None; Poisson models adjusted in two steps: (1) age, sex, race/ethnicity; (2) plus education, US census region, cigarette smoking history, other combustible tobacco, ever use of heroin, inhalants or hallucinogens, body mass index, and self-reported hypertension, high cholesterol, heart failure, heart attack, stroke and diabetes.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Within-category smoking intensity (the top pack-year category is open-ended, and former smokers have time since quitting but not pack-years), occupational and household exposures, income, allergy and family history, marijuana and second-hand smoke in the main models, and any change in e-cigarette or cigarette use after baseline.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Ever use of heroin, inhalants or hallucinogens: 4.0% of people who had never used e-cigarettes and 15.8% of those who currently used them (Table 1); adjusted for.

outcomes.instruments: Self-report at each wave of a diagnosis of COPD, emphysema, chronic bronchitis or asthma by a physician or other health professional in the past 12 months; incident if first reported over follow-up in someone without a history at baseline. A composite counts any of the four.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors state the survey items have been validated against direct clinical observation and widely used (references 38 to 40, not read). No lung function or medical records were used.
outcomes.operationalization: Incident respiratory condition = first self-reported diagnosis over Waves 2 to 4.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; five outcomes, three e-cigarette contrasts, two subsample analyses and six sensitivity analyses.

analysis.effect_sizes: Cases: asthma 804, emphysema 336, COPD 573, chronic bronchitis 948; 1,460 people (6.8%) with at least one. Multivariable incidence rate ratios against never use, ever / former / current: any respiratory condition 1.28 (95% CI 1.10-1.48) / 1.28 (1.09-1.51) / 1.31 (1.08-1.59); chronic bronchitis 1.33 (1.12-1.59) / 1.31 (1.08-1.58) / 1.33 (1.06-1.67); emphysema 1.54 (1.12-2.12) / 1.42 (1.01-2.01) / 1.69 (1.15-2.49); COPD 1.62 (1.28-2.04) / 1.66 (1.29-2.12) / 1.57 (1.15-2.13); asthma 1.24 (1.01-1.53) / 1.19 (0.95-1.50) / 1.32 (1.01-1.72). Multivariable-adjusted rates per 1,000 person-years, any respiratory condition: never 20.41 (18.65-22.17), former 26.12 (22.34-29.89), current 26.68 (21.83-31.52) (editors' calculation: about 2.0 against 2.6 to 2.7 new diagnoses per 100 people per year). The age-sex-race-adjusted ratios were much larger (any condition 2.14 ever; COPD 5.03; emphysema 4.02) and fell once smoking and the other covariates were added. Restricted to people with good or better self-rated health (n = 18,649): former 1.21 (1.00-1.47), current 1.43 (1.14-1.80); to people with no chronic condition at baseline (n = 14,865): ever 1.20 (0.99-1.45), former 1.11 (0.90-1.37), current 1.40 (1.09-1.79).
analysis.covariates: See comparison.matching. Multiple imputation by chained equations (5 imputations) for missing exposure and covariates; Wave 2 sample weights.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned; analyses were run from February to July 2020. Six sensitivity analyses are described (extra adjustment for second-hand smoke, marijuana, childhood smoke exposure and smokeless tobacco; listwise deletion; replicate weights; Wave 4 panel weights; excluding people who ever smoked cigarettes; excluding all other tobacco), with results only in a supplement (eTable) that was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: Results for the sensitivity analyses and the dose-response (intensity, age at first use, established use) analyses are in the supplement only; the text says they were similar or highest in every-day, early-starting, established use without numbers.
analysis.power: Adequate for the composite (1,460 cases) and the single conditions in the whole sample; the 'no chronic condition' subsample has 808 cases, and the never-smoker analyses rest on few people who currently used e-cigarettes and had never smoked (401).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In US adults followed for up to about four years from 2013-2014, those who had ever used e-cigarettes at baseline (including people who had tried them briefly) had about 28% higher rates of newly reported respiratory diagnoses than those who never had, after adjustment for smoking history and other factors (rate ratio 1.28, 1.10 to 1.48); the ratio was similar for former use (1.28) and current use (1.31), was smaller than the unadjusted-for-smoking ratios, and for asthma the former-use estimate had an interval that included 1 (0.95 to 1.50). Among people with no chronic condition at baseline the former-use estimate was 1.11 (0.90 to 1.37) and the current-use estimate 1.40 (1.09 to 1.79).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Key Points and Conclusions state that e-cigarette use was associated with increased risk of respiratory disease 'independent of' cigarette smoking and other tobacco use, and that people who use them 'may experience increased rates'; the Discussion adds that the results strengthen the evidence for a role of e-cigarettes in lung disease and may inform counselling, and cites animal studies as showing plausibility of causation. The same paper states that causality could not be established, that exposure was baseline-only, and that smoking was adjusted by broad categories. The similar ratios for people who had only tried e-cigarettes briefly or had stopped (former use) and for current use are not discussed as a possible sign of confounding.

timeline.event: Bhatta and Glantz, PATH waves 1 to 3, composite respiratory outcome: the authors report 31% higher risk with former use and 29% with current use of e-cigarettes after adjustment; the same cohort, so not an independent replication (described in this paper's Discussion; not read).

A cross-sectional study of 705,159 respondents to the US Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System 2016 and 2017 reported 75% higher odds of COPD in people who currently used e-cigarettes and had never smoked cigarettes (described in this paper's Discussion; not read).
Berlowitz et al.: cardiovascular outcomes in the same cohort (card sc_berlowitz_2022).

replication.where_it_stands: The direction (higher rates of self-reported respiratory diagnoses in people who vape than in people who never have, after adjustment) is reported by two analyses of the same PATH cohort and a cross-sectional survey; independent cohorts with objectively measured lung outcomes were not read for this batch. Whether it reflects the products or the smoking history that precedes them is the open question.

funding.funder: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and US Food and Drug Administration Center for Tobacco Products (grants P50HL120163, U54HL120163-01 and 1K01HL154130); American Lung Association Public Policy Research Award (PP-702811). The printed role-of-funder statement says the funders had no role in design, conduct, analysis, writing or the decision to submit.
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: Kathuria is a section editor for tobacco dependence treatment in UpToDate. Blaha reports FDA grants during the study and personal fees from Regeneron, Novartis, Novo Nordisk, Bayer, Akcea, 89Bio, Zogenix, Tricida, Gilead and Amgen outside the submitted work. Robertson reports FDA and NIH grants during the study. Benjamin reports NIH and American Heart Association grants during the study. Stokes reports grants from Ethicon, a subsidiary of Johnson and Johnson, outside the submitted work. No other disclosures.
funding.affiliations_note: Boston University, Johns Hopkins, Vanderbilt, the American Heart Association Tobacco Regulation and Addiction Center and the University of Louisville. No tobacco or e-cigarette manufacturer funding is declared; the conflicts listed are pharmaceutical and device-company ties and a federal regulator's grants.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort that records e-cigarette use at every wave with frequency, device and nicotine content, smoking history in full (pack-years and years since quitting), and objectively measured lung function and imaging; with analyses in people who never smoked and in long-term former smokers separately, marginal structural models for time-varying use, and a comparison against people who stopped smoking without vaping.

domains.note: People who currently used e-cigarettes were far more likely to have smoked (84% against 28% of those who never used them) and to have used other drugs and tobacco; smoking history was adjusted by broad categories only, with an open-ended top pack-year band and no pack-years for former smokers, so residual confounding by smoking is plausible and would raise the e-cigarette group's rate. The reverse-causation sensitivity analyses (healthy subsamples) address only one direction, and results in never smokers are in a supplement not read.
Single baseline self-report; 'former' includes people who tried 1 or 2 puffs; later changes ignored; device and nicotine unknown.
Retention 73.5% by Wave 4, with exclusion of people lost by Wave 2; weighted to the Wave 2 sample.
People who start, stop or switch products after baseline are classed by baseline status; the authors note this limitation.
Multiple imputation of exposure and covariates; the authors say listwise deletion gave similar results (supplement not read).
Self-reported diagnoses, not adjudicated or checked against lung function; validity is cited, not shown.
No plan stated; sensitivity and intensity results only in a supplement; five outcomes without correction.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E overall is no milder than the worst domain, and residual confounding by smoking history is a serious concern in a group that is mostly current or former smokers. The cohort is large and national, the follow-up is prospective, the incidence is analysed rather than prevalence, and the authors tested reverse causation and several alternative weights; but the main effect is modest (rate ratios about 1.2 to 1.7) and the same size in people who had only tried e-cigarettes. It may be cited for the rate ratios and absolute adjusted rates as reported, as an association in a US cohort of 2013-2018; not for a causal effect, for a particular product, or for any conclusion about lung function or severe disease.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7662143 (all sections, Tables 1 to 3, figure legend, author notes, funding and conflict-of-interest statement, reference list; the Figure is an image and was not extracted; the supplement (eTable, eFigures 1 and 2) was not read)

key_findings.finding: 21,618 adults analysed: 14,213 never, 5,076 former (11.6% weighted) and 2,329 current (5.2%) e-cigarette use at baseline; 7,405 (16.8%) had ever used. Retention of the baseline cohort 83.2% (Wave 2), 78.4% (Wave 3), 73.5% (Wave 4).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Methods › Study Setting, 1st paragraph; Results › Baseline Characteristics and e-Cigarette Use Behavior, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Former use was defined as ever having used an e-cigarette, even 1 or 2 puffs, and not now; current use as every day or some days.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, footnote b; Methods › Assessment of e-Cigarette Use, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Baseline smoking: 16.0% of people who currently used e-cigarettes had never smoked cigarettes (401 people) against 72.1% of those who had never used them; 22.0%, 28.2% and 18.5% of the current-use group were current smokers with under 5, 5 to 20 and 20 or more pack-years; mean pack-years 13.4 (current use), 11.6 (former use), 5.6 (never used).
New diagnoses during follow-up: asthma 804, emphysema 336, COPD 573, chronic bronchitis 948; 1,460 respondents (6.8%) with at least one.
key_findings.locator: Results › e-Cigarette Use and Incident Respiratory Conditions, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Multivariable-adjusted incidence rate ratios against never use for any respiratory condition: ever 1.28 (95% CI 1.10-1.48), former 1.28 (1.09-1.51), current 1.31 (1.08-1.59). Adjusted rates per 1,000 person-years: never 20.41 (18.65-22.17), ever 26.06 (22.63-29.49), former 26.12, current 26.68 (21.83-31.52).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, 'Any respiratory condition' rows; Results › e-Cigarette Use and Incident Respiratory Conditions, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Multivariable-adjusted incidence rate ratios, ever / former / current e-cigarette use: chronic bronchitis 1.33 / 1.31 / 1.33; emphysema 1.54 / 1.42 / 1.69; COPD 1.62 / 1.66 / 1.57; asthma 1.24 (1.01-1.53) / 1.19 (0.95-1.50) / 1.32 (1.01-1.72). Adjusted rates per 1,000 person-years, never vs ever: COPD 6.48 vs 10.49; emphysema 3.74 vs 5.76; bronchitis 12.18 vs 16.23; asthma 10.73 vs 13.31.

The age-, sex- and race/ethnicity-adjusted ratios for ever use were 2.14 (any condition), 4.02 (emphysema) and 5.03 (COPD); they fell to 1.28, 1.54 and 1.62 after adjustment for smoking history and the other covariates.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, rows 'Age-, sex-, and race/ethnicity-adjusted IRR' and 'Multivariable-adjusted IRR'

key_findings.finding: Among people with good, great or excellent self-rated health (n = 18,649): former 1.21 (1.00-1.47), current 1.43 (1.14-1.80). Among people with no chronic condition at baseline (n = 14,865): ever 1.20 (0.99-1.45), former 1.11 (0.90-1.37), current 1.40 (1.09-1.79).
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Results › e-Cigarette Use and Incident Respiratory Conditions, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Exploratory analyses: the highest rates were in groups with every-day current use, first use before age 25 and established use; no significant interaction with sex; six sensitivity analyses (including excluding people who smoked cigarettes or used other tobacco) gave similar results to the main analysis. Values are in the supplement, not read.
key_findings.locator: Results › e-Cigarette Use and Incident Respiratory Conditions, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Statistical Analysis, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Authors' stated limits: self-reported exposure and diagnoses; observational data with relatively short follow-up, so causality could not be established; no time-varying exposure or confounding; device characteristics (generation, flavor) unavailable; lung function not measured. They also describe reverse causation (people with early symptoms switching to e-cigarettes or quitting) as a bias that could hide an association.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the asthma ratio for current use as 1.31 (95% CI 1.01-1.71); Table 2 gives 1.32 (1.01-1.72). The abstract's ratios for good self-rated health (former 1.00-1.46, current 1.14-1.79) also differ in the last digit from Table 3 (1.00-1.47, 1.14-1.80).

The sample for the composite outcome is 21,618 in the text and 21,640 in Table 2. The samples for single conditions are 25,202 (bronchitis), 23,686 (emphysema), 23,236 (COPD) and 20,914 (asthma): by the stated rule (excluding people with that condition at baseline) each should be at least as large as the composite sample, yet the asthma sample is 726 smaller than the composite, and the paper does not explain.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Baseline Characteristics, 1st paragraph; Table 2, condition headings
reporting_issues.consequence: The selection of participants for the asthma analysis cannot be reconstructed; the flow chart is in the supplement (not read).

reporting_issues.issue: For three conditions the former and current case counts do not sum to the ever-use count (bronchitis 274 + 144 = 418 vs 419; emphysema 92 + 62 = 154 vs 155; asthma 224 + 119 = 343 vs 344).
reporting_issues.consequence: Off by one (probably from multiple imputation of exposure); immaterial.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract prints '11 017 (491%)' men (49.1% in the Results) and a Results age band '66-64 years' (55-64); a sentence on the sample weights is repeated word for word in the Statistical Analysis section.
reporting_issues.locator: Abstract › Results; Results › Baseline Characteristics, 1st paragraph; Methods › Statistical Analysis, 3rd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The Key Points and Conclusions say the association is 'independent of' cigarette smoking and other tobacco, but this rests on categorical adjustment (with open-ended top pack-year band and no pack-years for former smokers) and on supplement-only sensitivity analyses; the former-use ratio (which includes 1 or 2 puffs) equals the current-use ratio.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should say 'after adjustment for smoking history', not 'independent of smoking', and should not call it an effect of e-cigarettes.
